index.title: The Rows a Training Step Changes
index.prompt: The running example ties its weights, so the embedding table both embeds the input tokens and makes the logits. After one step of gradient descent on the training text the cat sat on, how many of the eight rows of the table change?
index.answer: 8. At each position the logits' gradient is the vector of probabilities, with 1 taken off at the target. Every probability is positive, so every logit has a gradient, and since each logit is a final vector times a row of E, every row gets the sum over the three positions of its logit's gradient times that position's final vector. The rows of “the”, “cat” and “sat” also get a gradient through the lookup. In the running example the smallest change is to the row of “ran”, whose gradient has length 0.04. Step 2's rule that only the looked-up rows change holds for an input table on its own, not for a tied one.

theory.title: The Loss of a Longer Text
overview: The training text grows to "the cat sat on the". The model reads "the cat sat on" and makes four predictions, with the targets "cat", "sat", "on" and "the". Running the block on these four tokens gives "on", at the fourth position, the final vector $(-0.675,\ -0.796,\ -0.221,\ 1.692)$.

prompt.p: What is the loss, averaged over the four positions? Give three decimal places.

answer.p: The first three positions are the ones on this page. The causal mask keeps each of them from seeing "on", so their final vectors, probabilities and losses do not change: 3.906, 3.583 and 0.299.
The new position needs its logits, the dot products of its final vector with the eight rows of $E$:
The total is 32.138, so the probability of the target "the" is $0.509 / 32.138 = 0.01584$, and its loss is $-\log 0.01584 = 4.145$. The average over the four positions is

The model again gives "on" the most probability, 0.736, so the new target costs more than any of the first three. Dividing the four losses by 3, the number of positions on this page, would give 3.978. Every position with a target counts once, and the last input token, "on", has one.

theory.title: The Rows a Training Step Changes

prompt.p: The running example ties its weights: the table $E$ embeds the input tokens in Step 2 and makes the logits in Step 12. The model takes one step of gradient descent on the training text "the cat sat on", with its three predictions, "cat", "sat" and "on". How many of the eight rows of $E$ change?

choices.explain: Those are the rows that were looked up, and on the input side they are the only rows with a gradient, as Step 2 says. With weight tying E is also the output layer: every logit at every position is the dot product of that position's final vector with a row of E, so the loss reaches every row through the logits as well.

This adds the row of “on”, the one target that was not also an input, as if only the targets' logits mattered. The loss reads only the target's probability, but that probability divides by a sum over all eight tokens, so every logit gets a gradient: its probability, minus 1 for the target. Each row of E then gets the sum over the positions of its logit's gradient times that position's final vector.

At each position the logits' gradient is the vector of probabilities, with 1 taken off at the target. Every probability is positive, so every logit has a gradient, and since each logit is a final vector times a row of E, every row gets the sum over the three positions of its logit's gradient times that position's final vector. The rows of “the”, “cat” and “sat” also get a gradient through the lookup. In the running example the smallest change is to the row of “ran”, whose gradient has length 0.04. Step 2's rule that only the looked-up rows change holds for an input table on its own, not for a tied one.

theory.title: Word Order Without Position Values
overview: Remove Step 3 from the running example: the block reads the token embeddings with no position values added. Everything else stays, the causal mask included. Compare two inputs:

prompt.p: Show that after the block, "sat" has exactly the same vector in A and in B.

answer.p: Follow the row of "sat" through the block. Its query is made from its own embedding, which is the same in A and B. It is the last token, so the mask hides nothing from it, and it sees the keys and values of "the", "cat" and itself in both inputs, only listed in a different order.

Each of its scores depends on its query and on one key, so A and B give "sat" the same three scores, attached to the same three tokens. The softmax divides each $e^{s_j}$ by the sum of all three, and a sum does not depend on the order of its terms, so each token gets the same weight in A as in B. The output of each head is $\sum_j a_j v_j$, again the same terms in another order. So the row of "sat" in $M$ is the same.

Everything after attention works on each row alone: the residual addition, both LayerNorms and the feed-forward network. They receive the same row of "sat" in A and B, so they give the same result. With the running example's weights it is $(-1.319,\ -0.598,\ 1.140,\ 0.777)$ in both.

prompt.p: Now stack two copies of the block, with the same weights in both. Explain why "sat" can come out of the second block with different vectors in A and B.

answer.p: The argument of Part 1 needs the rows that "sat" attends to in a block to be the same in A and B, apart from their order. That holds for block 1, whose input is the bare embeddings, but not for block 2, whose input is block 1's output.

Look at the first two rows that block 1 hands on. The first token can see only itself, so its output depends on its own token alone: call it $f(\text{the})$ in A and $f(\text{cat})$ in B. The second token sees itself and the first: $g(\text{cat} \mid \text{the})$ in A and $g(\text{the} \mid \text{cat})$ in B. So in block 2, "sat" attends to $\{f(\text{the}), g(\text{cat} \mid \text{the})\}$ in A and to $\{f(\text{cat}), g(\text{the} \mid \text{cat})\}$ in B, plus its own row, which Part 1 showed is the same. These are different vectors, not the same vectors in another order, so nothing forces the outputs to agree.

With the running example's weights, "sat" leaves block 2 with $(-1.498,\ -0.275,\ 1.117,\ 0.656)$ in A and $(-1.510,\ -0.238,\ 1.137,\ 0.611)$ in B, and the logit of "on" is 2.430 in A against 2.358 in B. The difference comes from the mask: a token's output in block 1 depends on how many tokens it could see, so block 1 writes some information about position into the vectors, and block 2 can read it. Haviv et al. (2022) found that causal language models trained with no position values at all still learn to use word order this way.

prompt.p: Now remove the causal mask as well, so that every token attends to all three, as in an encoder. Show that then no number of blocks lets the vector of "sat" tell A from B.

answer.p: Show that one block without the mask treats a reordering of its input rows by reordering its output rows in the same way. Let $X_B$ be $X_A$ with rows 1 and 2 swapped.

list: Queries, keys and values are made row by row, so those of B are those of A with rows 1 and 2 swapped.

The score of one token against another depends only on the query of the first and the key of the second, so the scores of B are those of A with rows 1 and 2 swapped and columns 1 and 2 swapped. With no mask, no score is hidden, so this holds for every entry.
The softmax of a row does not depend on the order of its entries, so the weights move the same way, and each output $\sum_j a_{ij} v_j$ is the output of A for the same token.
The residual additions, the LayerNorms and the feed-forward network work on each row alone.

answer.p: So the output of the block for B is the output for A with rows 1 and 2 swapped, and the row of "sat", row 3, is the same. The output of block 1 for B is therefore again A's with two rows swapped, and the same argument applies to block 2, then block 3, and so on. After any number of blocks, "sat" has the same vector in A and B, so the model cannot tell the two orders apart there.

Without the mask, the model sees each text as a collection of tokens, and the position values of Step 3 are its only source of order. With the mask, some order leaks in through the different numbers of tokens each position can see, as Part 2 showed, but position values give it to every block directly.

theory.title: Sampling from the Running Example's Logits
overview: The running example gives these logits for the token after "the cat sat", the last row of Step 12, listed from the most to the least likely, as the lesson's own table does:

prompt.p: At temperature 1, what are the probabilities of "on" and of "sat", each to three decimals?

answer.p: Exponentiate each logit, then divide by the sum. Subtracting the largest logit, 3.197, from all of them first keeps the numbers readable: "on" becomes 0, "sat" becomes -1.667 and "dog" becomes -2.421, whose exponentials are 1, 0.189 and 0.089. All eight unnormalized weights add up to 33.001, and the two asked for are the largest:
These are the first two rows of the lesson's table. The ratio is $0.741 / 0.140 = 5.3$, and 5.3 is $e^{1.667}$, the logit gap: at temperature 1 a gap of 1.667 makes "on" 5.3 times as likely as "sat".

prompt.p: The temperature is set to 0.5. What is the probability of "on", to three decimals, and how many times more likely is "on" than "sat", to the nearest whole number? Which tokens does top-p 0.9 then keep?

answer.p: Dividing every logit by 0.5 doubles the gaps: the gap between "on" and "sat" grows from 1.667 to 3.334. Exponentiating the doubled logits gives unnormalized weights of 598.245 for "on" and 21.328 for "sat", summing to 624.994 over the whole vocabulary, so

"on" alone already passes 0.9, so the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities reach 0.9 is that one token, and sampling from it has no randomness left: "on" is drawn every time. The low temperature does the same job as top-p, and more strongly.

prompt.p: The temperature is set to 2. What is the probability of "on", to three decimals, and which tokens does top-p 0.9 keep?

answer.p: Dividing every logit by 2 halves the gaps: the gap between "on" and "sat" shrinks from 1.667 to 0.834. The unnormalized weights now add up to 11.472, of which "on" holds 4.946:

Adding the probabilities in the lesson's order gives cumulative sums of 0.431 for "on", 0.618 for "sat", 0.747 for "dog", 0.810 for "the", 0.869 for "ran" and 0.922 for "cat". The running total first reaches 0.9 at "cat", so top-p 0.9 keeps six tokens: "on", "sat", "dog", "the", "ran" and "cat". At temperature 1 the same top-p kept three, so warming the temperature makes top-p open the set much wider.

prompt.p: Still at temperature 2, top-k is set to 3. The kept probabilities are renormalized to sum to 1. What probability does each of the three kept tokens get, to three decimals? At which of the three temperatures do top-3 and top-p 0.9 pick the same set of tokens?

answer.p: Top-k keeps "on", "sat" and "dog", whose probabilities at temperature 2 add up to 0.431 + 0.187 + 0.128 = 0.747. Dividing each by that sum:

At temperature 1 the same step gives 0.783, 0.148 and 0.070, so the warm temperature spreads one fixed three-way choice far more evenly. The two strategies agree only at temperature 1, where the top three probabilities already sum to 0.947 and top-p 0.9 stops at "dog". At temperature 0.5 top-p keeps one token against top-k's three, and at temperature 2 it keeps six against three. Top-p tracks the model's confidence and top-k does not, which is the reason the two are often combined.

answer.result: 0.577, 0.251 and 0.172, and they agree only at temperature 1
